blocks.prompt: The Bird With a Net Under Its Chin
blocks.text: A pelican carries its fishing net with it. The net is a pouch of stretchy skin that hangs under its long bill. When the pelican wants a fish, it opens its bill under the water. The pouch swells out like a balloon full of water and fish. That is far too heavy to fly with, so the pelican squeezes the water out of the sides of its bill. Sometimes a gull lands on its head and tries to steal the fish while it waits. Then the pelican tips its bill up and swallows. The pouch flattens back under its chin, folded away until the next fish swims by.

blocks.prompt: Two Ways to Catch a Fish
blocks.text: There are eight kinds of pelican in the world, and they do not all fish the same way. The brown pelican hunts from the air. It flies above the sea, spots a fish below, then folds its wings and falls. It hits the water hard enough to stun the fish underneath it, and the shock would knock the breath out of most birds. The pelican is fine, because it has pockets of air under the skin of its chest that soften the landing and pop it straight back up to the surface like a cork. The American white pelican never dives at all. It works in a team. A line of white pelicans swims side by side, beating the water with their wings and driving the fish ahead of them into the shallows. When the fish have nowhere left to go, every pelican dips its bill at once. Two birds, two plans, one thing in common. Both of them scoop, and both of them tip the water out before they swallow.

blocks.prompt: The Dive That Should Break a Bird
blocks.text: People think a pelican stores fish in its pouch, the way you would carry lunch in a bag. It does not. The pouch, which scientists call the gular pouch, is a net. It has one job, and the job lasts about two seconds. A brown pelican fishes by falling. It cruises thirty or sixty feet above the water, watching for a shape below the surface, then tucks its wings back and drops. It can be moving forty miles an hour when it arrives. The pouch snaps open on impact and swells with as much as three gallons of seawater, along with whatever fish were unlucky enough to be inside it. Water is heavy. That mouthful weighs more than the rest of the bird. The pelican cannot fly with it and does not try. It sits on the surface with its bill tilted down and lets the water stream out of the edges, keeping the fish pinned inside. Only then does it lift its bill and swallow. The whole business should injure the bird, and for most birds it would. Pelicans have two defenses. The first is a layer of air sacs beneath the skin of the chest and neck, which cushions the blow and floats the bird back to the surface. The second is stranger. A brown pelican rotates its body to the left in the last moment of the dive. Scientists think this is protection: its windpipe and food pipe run down the right side of its neck, and the twist turns them away from the smash.

blocks.prompt: The Bird That Came Back
blocks.text: The pelican is an old design that still works. Eight species survive today, on every continent except Antarctica, and all of them share the same equipment: a hooked bill, a body built to float, and the gular pouch, a sling of bare skin stretched between the two halves of the lower bill. The pouch is not a pantry. It is a net that fills, drains, and empties within seconds. It has a second use in hot weather, when the bird ripples the bare skin to move air across it and shed heat, a trick called gular fluttering. A pelican cannot sweat, so it fans its own throat instead. What almost ended the brown pelican was not a predator or a storm. It was a chemical. From the 1940s onward, farmers across the United States sprayed DDT to kill insects. Rain carried it into rivers, rivers carried it to the coast, and it worked its way up the food chain until it reached the animals eating the fish. In pelicans it interfered with the way the body lays down calcium, and the eggshells came out thin. A parent pelican incubates its eggs by standing on them, warming them with its broad webbed feet. Shells that had been strong enough for millions of years now cracked under the weight of the bird trying to hatch them. Whole colonies raised nothing. On Anacapa Island off California, a survey in 1970 found hundreds of nests and almost no surviving chicks. The United States banned DDT in 1972. Nothing was rebuilt, no chick was rescued, no habitat was replanted. The poison simply stopped arriving, and the shells slowly thickened again. It took decades. In 2009 the brown pelican was removed from the endangered species list, and today they queue along fishing piers as though they had never left. The lesson is unglamorous and worth remembering. The most powerful thing people did for the pelican was to stop doing something.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Family Pelecanidae, 8 living species
A 30 million year old fossil bill matches the modern one
Dalmatian pelican: wingspan close to 11 feet
Brown pelicans twist left to shield the windpipe
Subcutaneous air sacs cushion the plunge
DDT ban 1972; delisted 2009

blocks.prompt: Thirty Million Years of Not Changing
blocks.text: In 2010, researchers described a fossil pelican pulled from thirty million year old deposits in southern France. The interesting thing about it was how boring it was. The bill was long, hooked at the tip, and clearly built to carry a pouch. Set beside the skull of a pelican fishing off a California pier this morning, it is close to indistinguishable. Thirty million years is an enormous span of time. Whole families of mammals have appeared, spread, and vanished inside it. The pelican simply kept its face. That tells you something about the design, so it is worth asking what the design actually does. The gular pouch is a sling of bare skin slung between the flexible arms of the lower bill. It is not a container for carrying food, whatever the old rhyme suggests. It is a net, and it works on a timer of roughly two seconds. A brown pelican locates a fish from as high as sixty feet, folds back its wings, and falls. It can strike the surface at speeds near forty miles an hour. On impact the bill gapes, the bill arms bow outward, and the pouch balloons to hold something like three gallons of seawater. Three gallons weighs more than the bird does. Flight is impossible in that state and the pelican does not attempt it. It surfaces, angles the bill downward, and lets the sea drain out through the gap along the edges while the fish stay trapped behind them. Gulls have learned this. They land on the pelican's head and try to rob the pouch during the few seconds it takes to drain. Then the bill tips skyward, the throat works once, and the net folds flat again. Surviving that dive is its own engineering problem. A bird is a fragile object and forty miles an hour into water is a serious collision. Pelicans carry a network of air sacs beneath the skin of the chest and throat, which spreads the force of impact and buoys the bird back to the surface almost immediately. Stranger still, a brown pelican rotates its body to the left in the final instant before it hits. The trachea and esophagus run down the right side of a pelican's neck, and the leading explanation is that the twist swings those soft tubes away from the blow. Nobody designed that. Birds that flinched the wrong way left fewer chicks. And yet this ancient, well solved animal was nearly finished off inside a single human lifetime. DDT, sprayed on American farmland from the 1940s, accumulated up the food chain and disrupted calcium deposition in pelicans. Their eggshells thinned. Since a pelican incubates by standing on its clutch and warming it with webbed feet, the parent broke its own eggs. Colonies produced almost nothing. The United States banned DDT in 1972, the poison stopped arriving, the shells recovered, and in 2009 the brown pelican was taken off the endangered species list. Thirty million years of engineering nearly undone by one chemical, and repaired not by cleverness but by restraint.
